content: 1. Referral to ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialists, as well as provider-assisted referral and social network-based approaches, are effective strategies for managing sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Provider-supported approaches are particularly effective and should be prioritized or encouraged whenever feasible. 2. Expedited Partner Therapy (EPT) can be considered as part of partner services for certain curable STIs, such as chlamydia or gonorrhea. This involves providing treatment to the sexual partners of individuals diagnosed with these infections without requiring the partners to undergo a clinical examination. 3. Linking sexual partners to STI management services is a critical component of comprehensive STI care. Integration of STI partner services into broader health programs, such as those addressing HIV and viral hepatitis, is recommended to enhance service delivery. 4. Social network testing services may be offered as an additional approach to HIV testing within a comprehensive package of care and prevention. This approach involves enlisting individuals to encourage and offer testing to others in their social, sexual, or drug-injecting networks, without requiring disclosure of their own test results. 5. Offering self-testing as an option through social network testing approaches, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), may increase acceptability, feasibility, and uptake. However, the use of self-testing should be tailored to the specific context, epidemiology, and available resources. 6. Provider-assisted partner services should be offered to all individuals with HIV-associated tuberculosis (TB) as part of a voluntary, comprehensive package of HIV testing, care, and prevention services. This approach is strongly recommended based on moderate-certainty evidence. 7. Regular, free, voluntary, and confidential counseling and testing for HIV and TB should be implemented in collaboration with health workers’ representatives. This should include addressing sexual and reproductive health issues and intensified case finding among the families of health workers with TB. 8. Household contacts and other close contacts of individuals with TB should be systematically screened for TB. Biological children of parents with HIV should routinely be offered HIV testing services (HTS) and linked to treatment or prevention services if found to have HIV or be at high risk of infection. 9. Family and household testing services, often referred to as index testing, should be offered to the children of clients with HIV when the HIV status of the child is unknown. This approach enables families to access care as a unit and may improve retention and convenience for families affected by HIV. 10. Partner services involve trained providers offering voluntary testing to the sexual and/or drug-injecting partners of consenting individuals with HIV, STIs, or viral hepatitis. These services can be delivered through various methods, including partner referral and provider-assisted partner services. 11. Enhanced partner referral involves the use of support tools, such as written information, referral slips, web-based messaging, or provision of HIV self-testing kits, to facilitate the offer of testing by clients to their partners. 12. Delayed assisted partner services involve an agreement between the client and a trained provider to suggest testing to partners within a specified period. If the partners do not access testing or contact the provider within that period, the provider directly contacts the partners to offer voluntary testing. 13. Provider-assisted partner services, also known as index testing or assisted partner notification, involve trained providers contacting partners of clients, with the client’s consent, to inform them of potential exposure and offer voluntary testing and additional services. 14. Social network testing services leverage individuals, including those newly diagnosed or testing negative, to encourage and offer testing to others in their social, sexual, or drug-injecting networks. This approach addresses confidentiality concerns and broadens the reach of testing to include diverse populations. 15. Evidence suggests that social network testing approaches may increase the uptake of HIV testing among sexual partners and social contacts, reach more first-time testers, and diagnose more people with HIV. No social harms or adverse events have been identified following social network approaches. 16. Social network testing services are generally highly acceptable and feasible across different settings and populations. They may require fewer resources and provider time compared to community outreach or some forms of partner services. 17. Peer-supported groups may increase testing uptake compared to community outreach alone. Self-testing can also increase uptake and linkage but may be costlier, and some users may prefer other testing approaches. 18. Family and household testing services can be delivered through a combination of facility-based and community-based services. Integration of services across disease areas should be considered to maximize impact and efficiency. 19. In the United Republic of Tanzania, social network testing services were implemented in both community and health facility settings to reach key and vulnerable populations. Test promoters were identified through peers and provided with coupons to share with their social contacts, who could then access testing at health facilities. 20. Social network testing in health facilities complemented provider-assisted partner services by enabling individuals to reach social network members at substantial risk. This approach was used as an adjunct to enhance the reach and effectiveness of testing services.
